name: Algae Green
lede: Algae Green is a vivid green named directly for pond algae, recorded in the 2010 xkcd color-naming survey.

sections.title: Straight from the pond
sections.body: The name is a plain nature word: algae, the green growth found on still water [1]. It entered ColorHub's library from the 2010 xkcd survey, in which thousands of people typed free-text names for colors shown on screen, rather than from any of the historical pigment or dye dictionaries [1]. No older record of the exact name turns up in the sources consulted [1]. The nearest named greens are [[emerald]] and [[shamrock]], with [[seaweed]] and [[green-crayola]] close by on the duller, darker side [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: No painting in our 23,781-painting archive holds this exact green covering at least one percent of its canvas, as photographed [3]. That describes this particular archive of historical paintings, not the color's presence in the wider world; bright, saturated greens like this are rare in aged, varnished canvases generally [3]. Bright, saturated greens like this one simply do not survive well in aged paint and varnish, which is part of why the archive shows none [3].

notes.cite: ColorHub color library: xkcd color survey, 2010
ColorHub color graph: nearest-neighbor computation over named colors (CIE Lab ΔE)
ColorHub archive (23,781 paintings), computed match, as photographed

questions.q: Algae Green's name comes from which kind of source?
Why might a bright green like Algae Green be rare in old paintings?
choices: Aged, varnished paint rarely keeps such saturated greens
Algae was banned as a pigment source
Green pigments did not exist before 1900
questions.answer: Aged, varnished paint rarely keeps such saturated greens

openers: Algae Green is almost never found in historical paintings, as photographed.
